extracted.intended_audience: research mathematicians in combinatorial/discrete geometry and related areas
extracted.subtask_description: A research-paper-level construction and proof showing that Borsuk's conjecture fails in high dimensions; includes definitions, combinatorial reductions/conjectures, key theorems used (Frankl–Wilson, Frankl–Rödl), and an explicit combinatorial construction producing the counterexample.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of f(d)
rubrics_metrics.description: Let f(d) be the smallest number so that every set in R^d of diameter 1 can be partitioned into f(d) sets of diameter smaller than 1.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the central quantity studied in the paper; it formalizes the partitioning problem that Borsuk's conjecture addresses. The paper repeatedly refers to and bounds f(d).

rubrics_metrics.name: Borsuk's conjecture (statement)
rubrics_metrics.description: Problem 1 (Borsuk). Is it true that every set of diameter one in R^d can be partitioned into d + 1 closed sets of diameter smaller than one? The conjecture that this is true has come to be called Borsuk’s conjecture.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Historical context: proved for dimensions 2 and 3 and for centrally symmetric convex bodies and smooth convex bodies (references cited). The vertices of the regular simplex and the d-dimensional Euclidean ball show the lower bound f(d) ≥ d+1 in these contexts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Known upper-bound results on f(d)
rubrics_metrics.description: Cited results giving upper bounds on f(d): Lassak proved f(d) ≤ 2d (and other refined bounds appear: Schramm’s bound and Bourgain–Lindenstrauss proofs/reproofs).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These references and bounds provide context and contrast to the paper's lower-bound construction; see cited works [14], [16], [3] and survey references [9,1,4].

rubrics_metrics.name: Combinatorial reduction conjecture (Larman's formulation)
rubrics_metrics.description: Conjecture 1. Let K be a family of k-subsets of {1,2,...,n} such that every two members of K have t elements in common. Then K can be partitioned into n parts so that in each part every two members have (t + 1) elements in common.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This illustrates how Borsuk's conjecture can be reduced, for certain 0-1 vector sets of constant weight, to a pure combinatorial partitioning statement. The paper refers to earlier suggestions by Erdős and Larman that combinatorial configurations might yield counterexamples.

rubrics_metrics.name: Main theorem (Kahn & Kalai)
rubrics_metrics.description: Theorem 1. For large enough d, f(d) ≥ (1.2)√d by constructing an appropriate family of sets.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the paper's primary result: a lower bound on f(d) that disproves Borsuk's conjecture for sufficiently large dimensions. (Text uses the notation '(1.2)√d' as stated.) The proof proceeds by constructing a family of sets and applying combinatorial intersection theorems.

rubrics_metrics.name: Frankl–Wilson intersection theorem (used as tool)
rubrics_metrics.description: Theorem 2 (Frankl and Wilson). Let k be a prime power and n = 4k. Let K be a family of n/2-subsets of {1,2,...,n}, so that no two sets in the family have intersection of size n/4. Then |K| ≤ 2 · (n − 1) / (n/4 − 1).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The paper invokes this combinatorial intersection bound to control the size of families avoiding a particular intersection size; it is a central ingredient in showing many members of the constructed family must realize the minimal intersection and therefore force large chromatic/partition numbers. (Formula reproduced as in the paper; see original Frankl–Wilson reference [8] for the precise binomial-coefficient formulation.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Frankl–Rödl bound (related tool)
rubrics_metrics.description: Theorem 3 (Frankl and Rödl). Let n be a positive integer divisible by four. Let K be a family of n/2-subsets of {1,2,...,n} such that no two sets in the family have intersection of size n/4. Then |K| ≤ (1.99)n.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This related result (cited) gives an alternative quantitative bound on the size of such intersection-free families; the paper cites it for context and comparison. (Text prints '(1.99)n' — see original source [7] for exact exponential formulation.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Construction of the family K (explicit combinatorial construction)
rubrics_metrics.description: Let V = {1,2,...,m}, with m = 4k and k a prime power. Let W be the set of pairs of elements in V. For every partition P = {A,B} of V with |A| = 2k let S(A,B) be the set of all pairs which contain one element from A and one from B. Let K = {S(A,B) : |A| = 2k}. Thus K is a family of (m^2/4)-subsets of an m(m−1)/2-set.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The construction produces a large family of edge-sets coming from balanced bipartitions; the minimal intersection between two such S(A,B) occurs when |A ∩ C| = k. Applying Frankl–Wilson to subfamilies shows that any partition avoiding the minimal intersection needs many parts, yielding the claimed lower bound on f(d). The paper traces how this construction gives the quantitative bound (stated as exceeding (1.203)√d for large d=(m choose 2) − 1).

rubrics_metrics.name: Implication for chromatic number g(d)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Frankl–Wilson theorem implies that, if g(d) is the smallest number so that R^d can be colored by g(d) colors such that no two points of the same color are distance one apart, then g(d) ≥ (1.2)d.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The paper connects the partitioning problem (f(d)) to the related distance–graph chromatic number g(d), using the combinatorial intersection theorems to derive lower bounds for coloring problems in Euclidean space.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quantitative consequences and explicit dimensions with counterexamples
rubrics_metrics.description: The authors' construction shows that Borsuk’s conjecture is false for d = 1,325 and for every d > 2,014.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This remark gives explicit (computed) dimensions in which the counterexample exists, indicating the construction is effective enough to produce concrete small-dimensional failures (subject to the arithmetic in the construction).

rubrics_metrics.name: Open problems and remarks about asymptotics
rubrics_metrics.description: Remark: It would be of considerable interest to have a better understanding of the asymptotic behavior of log f(d). At the moment, we cannot distinguish the asymptotic behavior of f(d) from that of g(d). Also of interest would be counterexamples in small dimensions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The authors highlight open directions: tighten asymptotic bounds on f(d) and g(d), find smaller-dimensional counterexamples, and further study related combinatorial partition conjectures (e.g., Larman's conjecture for t=1).

rubrics_metrics.name: Contextual references and prior work (criteria for applicability)
rubrics_metrics.description: Surveyed and cited prior results (Borsuk [2]; Danzer [5]; work of Larman, Lassak, Schramm, Bourgain–Lindenstrauss, Frankl–Wilson, Frankl–Rödl, etc.) that establish cases where Borsuk's conjecture holds or provide upper/lower bounds.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These references set criteria for when the conjecture had been verified (low dimensions, centrally symmetric or smooth convex bodies) and previously known bounds; they also point the reader to the combinatorial tools used in the new construction.
